content: Albinism is a hereditary condition caused by genetic mutations that disrupt melanin synthesis. Despite this disruption, the number of melanocytes remains intact. Melanin is a pigment responsible for skin, hair, and eye coloration, as well as protection against ultraviolet radiation. The condition is classified into several types, including oculocutaneous albinism (OCA), Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome (HPS), Chediak-Higashi syndrome (CHS), and ocular albinism (OA). Patients with albinism exhibit both cutaneous and ocular manifestations. Cutaneous features include hypopigmented or white hair, skin, and eyelashes. Ocular features include photophobia, reduced visual acuity, pink-colored eyes, hypopigmentation of the iris, refractive errors, strabismus, nystagmus, foveal hypoplasia, and iris transillumination. Management of albinism involves addressing both cutaneous and ocular symptoms. Patients are advised to avoid prolonged sun exposure and undergo regular dermatological evaluations to monitor for skin cancer. Corrective lenses are used to address refractive errors, while tinted lenses or glasses can help alleviate photophobia. Older children may benefit from bifocal or low-vision aids, while infants with strabismus may require eye patching. In cases of nystagmus, contact lenses or eye surgery may be considered. Additionally, nitisinone has been shown to improve pigmentation in individuals with OCA1. Historically, albinism was first identified in 1908 by Sir Archibald Edward Garrod, a British physician. Initially, it was thought to result from a lack of melanocytes. However, by the late 1950s, it was established that albinism is caused by tyrosinase enzyme inactivity, which impairs the conversion of tyrosine to melanin. Melanocytes, derived from neural crest ectoderm, are present in hair follicles, skin, eyes, and the inner ear. These cells produce melanin through a process involving the enzyme tyrosinase, which converts tyrosine into DOPA, dopaquinone, and eventually melanin. Mutations in the tyrosinase enzyme are the primary cause of albinism. In individuals with albinism, abnormal decussation of optic nerve fibers at the optic chiasm leads to monocular vision, often presenting as strabismus. In ocular albinism, the absence of macular pigment and foveal hypoplasia further contribute to reduced visual acuity. Albinism must be differentiated from other rare conditions, such as Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome, Chediak-Higashi syndrome, Griscelli syndrome, Waardenburg syndrome type II, Vici syndrome, Tietz albinism-deafness syndrome, Angelman syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome, Cross-McKusick-Breen syndrome, achromatopsia, Aland Island eye disease (Forsius-Eriksson syndrome), aniridia, and congenital nystagmus. Among the various types of albinism, oculocutaneous albinism type 2 (OCA2) is the most prevalent. The risk of albinism is higher in individuals with a positive family history of the condition. Genetic sequence analysis can be performed for individuals with a familial predisposition to albinism. Complications of albinism include an increased risk of skin cancer, sunburn, reduced visual acuity, and psychosocial challenges such as poor self-image and social isolation, which may lead to depression. Despite these challenges, individuals with albinism have a normal life expectancy and do not experience developmental delays or intellectual disabilities. Diagnosis of albinism involves a thorough history and physical examination. Cutaneous findings include hypopigmented or white hair, skin, and eyelashes, while ocular findings include photophobia, reduced visual acuity, pink eyes, and hypopigmentation of the iris. Ocular physical examination may reveal refractive errors, strabismus, nystagmus, foveal hypoplasia, iris transillumination, and decreased iris pigmentation. Cutaneous pigmentation can range from white to light brown. Laboratory tests for albinism include hair bulb assays to assess tyrosinase activity, genetic sequence testing (the most definitive diagnostic method), bleeding tests for suspected Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome, and evaluation of polymorphonuclear leukocyte function in suspected Chediak-Higashi syndrome. Imaging studies such as macular optical coherence tomography can be used in young patients with nystagmus and foveal abnormalities to determine the underlying cause. Ophthalmological evaluation and visual-evoked potential testing are also important diagnostic tools. There are no findings associated with albinism on electrocardiograms, X-rays, CT scans, MRIs, or echocardiography/ultrasound. Treatment of albinism includes medical and surgical interventions. Medical management involves sun protection, regular dermatological evaluations, corrective lenses for refractive errors, tinted glasses for photophobia, and low-vision aids for older children. Eye patching may be used in infants to reduce strabismus, while contact lenses or eye surgery may be considered for nystagmus. Nitisinone can improve pigmentation in OCA1. Surgical options, such as eye muscle surgery, may improve ocular alignment and vision in severe cases, although it may not significantly improve strabismus due to the lack of necessary ocular connections. Primary prevention includes genetic counseling for couples with a family history of albinism or parents of children with albinism who are considering future pregnancies. There is no secondary prevention for albinism.
